## The status badge {#status-legend}

Every conjecture on this site carries one small badge showing how far it has got. Click any badge,
anywhere, to come back here.

The badge is worked out from six fields on the conjecture's own page, always the same way, and nobody
picks it by hand. It answers two questions at once: **how solid is the statement**, and **how far has
the proof got**.

The reason it treats those as two separate questions is worth spelling out, because it is the whole
design. You can write a conjecture out in Lean and have a machine verify a proof of it, and still have
proved nothing about the conjecture -- because the Lean version might not say the same thing as the
English one. So "somebody checked that the Lean matches the English" is tracked as its own signal, not
as a footnote.

### What the parts mean

**Which way it points is not a score.** A badge can say the work *disproves* the statement rather than
proving it. That never changes either score, and it cannot: how well established a piece of work is,
and which way it points, are different questions. A machine-checked disproof is exactly as finished as
a machine-checked proof. You also cannot claim a disproof without one: setting `proof_direction:
refutes` while the proof is still open is rejected when the site is built, because suspecting something
is false refutes nothing.

**If you cannot see the colours.** Red and green are the classic pair colour-blind readers cannot
separate. At the top of the proof scale the cross does the job on its own, so the badge still works in
black and white. Lower down -- a disproof drafted but not yet in Lean -- colour really is the only
visual difference, and the honest answer is that colour is not the only channel: the badge's caption
and its screen-reader label both say "Refutation" instead of "Proof", and the one-line summary next to
it is expected to say so in words. Read those rather than the hue.

### The six fields

**The statement half** (the outer ring) comes from three fields: who wrote the English version
(`statement_informal`), whether anyone has written it in Lean and who (`statement_formal`), and whether
anyone has checked that the Lean says the same thing as the English, and who (`statement_match`). Those
combine into a statement score from 0 (written by an AI, not in Lean) to 5 (written, put into Lean, and
checked, all by people).

**The proof half** (the inner disc) comes from three more: whether there is a written proof and who
wrote it (`proof_informal`), whether anyone reviewed it (`proof_review`, which stops mattering once
there is a machine-checked proof), and whether there is a finished Lean proof (`proof_formal` -- finished
meaning no `sorry` left standing in for a missing step). Those combine into a proof score from 0
(nobody has tried) to 4 (checked by machine). At 4 it stops mattering who wrote it, because the proof
checker is what decides.

### Reading a badge

The ring's colour is the statement score. Its line style repeats the same information a second way, so
it survives black and white: dotted means nobody has checked the Lean against the English, dashed means
an AI checked, solid means a person checked. The disc's colour is the proof score, with a mark in the
middle (`– · • ● ✓`) as a second channel again. Everything turns red, at the same lightness, when the
work disproves the statement instead of proving it, and the top mark becomes `✗`. A thin gold halo, which this site calls the *seal*,
appears only when a person has confirmed the Lean matches *and* the proof, or the disproof, is checked
by machine. Hover over any badge for the full status in plain words.

Five examples, from nothing done to fully checked, the last two pointing in opposite directions:

```{=html}

<tbody>
<tr><td><svg class='cj-status-badge' viewBox='0 0 32 32' width='28' height='28' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img'><title>Statement: AI-written, not yet formalized. This is where every new conjecture on this site starts</td></tr>

Proof: human draft, human-reviewed, not yet formalized.</title><circle cx='16' cy='16' r='13' fill='none' stroke-width='4' class='cj-ring-3' stroke-dasharray='5,3'/><circle cx='16' cy='16' r='8' class='cj-disc-3'/><text x='16' y='17' text-anchor='middle' dominant-baseline='central' class='cj-glyph' font-size='9'>●</text></svg></td><td>An AI confirmed the Lean matches, and a person reviewed the written proof. Gold halo</td></tr>
<tr><td><svg class='cj-status-badge cj-refuted' viewBox='0 0 32 32' width='28' height='28' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img'><title>Statement: human-written, human-formalized, human-matched against the informal statement. It gets the gold halo too, because the halo is about the checking being complete, not about the answer</td></tr>

```

To change a conjecture's status, edit the `status.*` fields in its `c/<id>/index.qmd` (the six above,
plus `proof_direction` if the work disproves rather than proves), then run `python3
scripts/status_badge.py` from the repository root. That regenerates the badge in two places: the
`status_badge:` field and the copy in the page body between the `<!-- status:start -->` and
`<!-- status:end -->` markers. Never edit `status_badge:` by hand.

## Difficulty {#difficulty-legend}

Every conjecture also carries a difficulty grade, shown as an italic tag next to its other tags, with
the reason on hover.

**It measures one thing, not three.** It measures *how far the conjecture is from techniques that
already exist*: what a solution would have to invent. It is deliberately not how much effort a solution
would take, because that depends on who is doing the work and with what. And it is deliberately not the
chance of it being solved by some date, which a handful of conjectures cannot possibly calibrate and
which no honest grader could defend. Reading it as either of those will mislead you.

The first of those two is tracked separately, and only for one kind of worker:
[attackability](/problems/attackability/index.qmd) estimates the effort for a machine with a fixed
budget. It is a different number and it does not feed this one. A conjecture can be `new-idea` here and
easy to attack there, or `adaptation` here and out of reach there. They disagree often enough that
treating them as one scale would mislead you in both directions.

| Grade | What it says |
|---|---|
| `routine` | A standard technique works as it stands. |
| `adaptation` | An existing technique has a visible route, with a real obstacle on it. |
| `new-idea` | Nothing in the literature gets there. Something unpublished is needed. |
| `barrier` | A published result says techniques of this kind cannot suffice. |

**Who graded it.** Every grade records whether a person or a machine made the call, and the tag shows
`(ai)` where a machine did. As everywhere on this site, a machine may never mark its own work as a
person's, and a person's assessment replaces a machine's openly rather than quietly. Where the evidence
is thin the grade rounds towards *harder than it looks*, on the same principle as the badge: it may
understate what is known, never overstate it.

Every grade comes with a one-sentence reason, and the reason is the part worth checking. A grade you
cannot argue with is decoration, not evidence, so the reason is required and a conjecture without one
fails the build.

## Where the badge appears

The same badge, ring and disc together, appears in listing tables and at the top of each conjecture's
own page, just above the Statement / Proof / Formal Artifact tabs.

## What the badge cannot tell you

The badge is deliberately narrow. It is worked out from those six fields and nothing else, and it always
will be. That means it cannot call a result settled before a machine has checked it, and its caption is
necessarily short. Two things beside it fill the gap.

**The one-line summary** (`status_summary`) is required, and appears next to the badge in every listing
table, so you can scan a page of conjectures without opening each one.

**The category** matters here too. Conjectures marked solved, or marked as test cases, exist on this
site precisely because the badge alone would make a result that is proved but not yet in Lean look
identical to one nobody has touched. [c/0004](/c/0004/) is a real example: it has an informal proof, its
badge is still low, and it is the category and the summary that actually say so.

Each conjecture page also lists its open obligations: the specific things still outstanding, such as
steps nobody has verified, files nobody has audited, Lean statements nobody has matched, or missing
sanity checks. How many are open is its own column in listing tables.

In short: **the badge and its caption summarise; the summary and the category say what the badge
cannot.**
